214(b) refused twice; the first refusal also triggered revocation of her existing valid B1/B2 tourist visa; second interview consisted of only 3 basic questions with no documents reviewed despite bringing an updated I-20, financial records and a university support letter

214(b), marked as failure to qualify for reasons other than failure to show ties -- despite a strong financial sponsor profile (father, roughly 100K+/year income) and multiple university scholarship offers, had no prior international travel and no US relatives
IRCC R216(1)(b) - officer not satisfied applicant would leave Canada at the end of the intended stay; reapplying for a different program at a different institution

214(b) - insufficient ties to the UK despite a new job starting, a small business started this year, a 12-month lease, and family in the UK. Status flipped from 'Approved' to 'Refused' after additional administrative-processing screening, following a 2025 ESTA overstay and two earlier B1/B2 refusals in Oct 2025. Illustrates that CEAC's 'Approved' status is not final - a case can still be refused in a later review stage even after verbal/system approval.

214(b) presumed immigrant intent - despite 2 years of stable employment, filed income tax returns, and personal assets in India, denied for the second time (Feb 2026) for a sibling's US wedding trip; officer only asked about travel plans before refusing. Forum consensus: unmarried women who are siblings of an already-immigrating/approved family member face extra suspicion of intent to stay.

212(a)(2)(A) crime involving moral turpitude (an old juvenile-era burglary/theft TIC believed to qualify for the petty-offense exception) plus a 214(b) stacked on top; officer barely asked about ties despite 40 years in the same home. A 'Taken Into Consideration' (TIC) offense can count as an uncharged admission that defeats the petty-offense exception, and 214(b) is often added automatically to criminal-inadmissibility refusals to block the waiver route.

214(b) - presumed immigrant intent as the spouse of a US citizen; despite living apart with stable local employment, an apartment owned by the US-citizen husband, and two young children in local school, the US-citizen spousal tie was read as pulling toward the US rather than the home country. Illustrates that having a USC spouse abroad can hurt, not help, a B1/B2 case.

Approved despite openly admitting to the officer she owned no farmland or property tying her to the Philippines; daughter (petitioner) was a green card holder for only 2 years with no kids yet. 4-5 well-crafted follow-up questions, no red flags on background check. Suggests officers weigh the whole picture (age, health, honesty, family circumstances) rather than a strict ties checklist.

214(b) presumed - denied after a roughly 3-question interview lasting 2-3 minutes at the Manila embassy, no detailed reason given; family suspected the decision was effectively made from the DS-160 before the interview even started (three applicants ahead of her were also denied in quick succession).

214(b) presumed (no reason given at the window) - trip was framed around visiting for a grandchild's 1st birthday, a pattern consulates reportedly read as a likely childcare/overstay risk for grandparents of young children, compounded by modest income.

214(b) presumed - interview ended abruptly after the wife misspoke that her husband's business was 'located' in America (he is actually a mostly-retired remote writer based in Thailand); the officer cut off the interview at that single answer and never asked about her own ties (business license, commercial lease, home under construction, family). Shows one early answer touching on the US-citizen spouse can end the interview before the applicant's own ties are even considered.

Approved despite being married to a US citizen (a factor that sinks many other applicants in this dataset) - interviewed in Bolivia rather than Chile; forum poster believed a large part of the approval was simply not being a national of the higher-risk country (Bolivia) where the interview took place, since nearly everyone ahead of her in the Bolivia line was denied in 2-3 questions. Suggests nationality/interview-post risk profile can outweigh the 'married to a USC' red flag.

Renewal denied after 10 years of fully compliant B2 use; consulate seemed to flag that her original visa had been issued just 1 day before she turned 18, treated as a red flag. The trip's purpose (helping her sister after a new baby) risked reading as impermissible childcare/nanny work, and other members noted a letter of invitation tends to hurt B-visa cases rather than help since there is no 'sponsorship' concept for B visas.

Originally denied a B2 from Brazil for insufficient ties; later became a dual EU (Portuguese) citizen and tried ESTA instead, but ESTA was also denied because it is linked to the same biometric identity record (name, DOB, photo) as the earlier B2 refusal. A new passport/nationality does not erase a US visa refusal history.

214(b) - being a Nigerian national already living outside Nigeria (in Qatar) was itself read as suggestive of immigrant intent; Nigeria has an unusually high (~50%) B-visa refusal rate, and single women of marrying age face extra scrutiny. Interview lasted only two questions before refusal.

214(b) - despite owning property (including a rental property) and strong stated ties (retired, non-English speaking, extended family nearby), both parents were denied; their daughter's US green card status was seen as the dominant pull factor. Forum also flagged that unpaid childcare help for a new grandchild is technically impermissible 'work' on a B1/B2 and can itself be a red flag.

Denied not primarily for a pandemic-era overstay (which had documented extenuating circumstances) but because two earlier, fully legal 6-month stays (within visa terms, sanctioned at the port of entry) back-to-back over several years were read by the officer as 'abusing' the B2 as a long-term living arrangement. Unpaid childcare for relatives' kids while staying with family was also treated as unauthorized work (displacing a US nanny). Shows that even fully-within-limits repeated 6-month stays can themselves become grounds for a future denial.

214(b), twice - a 22-year-old with no convictions (two arrests as a minor/young adult, both resulting in No Further Action) was refused twice; the first interview required a 221(g) for a Subject Access Request (SAR) since he'd only brought an ACRO 'No Trace' report, and despite submitting the SAR he was told his 'lack of disclosure regarding his complete criminal history' didn't satisfy requirements. Shows a mere arrest history with zero convictions can still sink a young, tie-light applicant, and providing the wrong type of police document can be read as non-disclosure.

214(b) - two children in the process of being adopted by US-citizen parents were denied tourist visas for a stopover en route to the parents' new jobs in Canada; consulate cited insufficient ties to their home country, and the interviewer was reportedly critical/condescending about the multi-year gap before the family lived together (delayed by COVID and court process), and did not review proof of the parents' Canadian job offers.

214(b)/possible misrepresentation flag - first B2 application (Jan 2024) was denied for lack of ties, citing a trip with his brother and no family in the US; after marrying the US-based petitioner mid-year, he reapplied months later mentioning the marriage, but the officer accused him of 'lying' about the earlier claim of no US family ties and denied him again without letting him explain. Shows that reapplying within the same year with a materially different story can be read as prior misrepresentation/fraud rather than a genuine change in circumstances, and that a US citizen spouse is treated as a pull factor, not a tie that helps a tourist visa case.

Approved, but the visa was annotated/restricted to a single entry and one specific US state with only 1-year validity (rather than a typical multi-year B2), despite a strong individual profile (full-time student, well-off family, prior fully-compliant J1 visa, extensive international travel, no legal issues). Forum consensus: this reflects broad nationality-level risk profiling (Mexican nationals' aggregate illegal-crossing/overstay rates) overriding individual merits - even a strong applicant can get a heavily limited visa instead of a full one.

214(b) - 'not enough assets to tie her back to China,' despite being elderly and retired, which forum folklore treats as an automatic 'slam dunk' tie. Counters that folklore: age alone isn't sufficient, assets still matter, and nationality (China vs. Philippines, per other members' experience) appears to carry very different baseline odds for an otherwise similar retired-parent profile.

212(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) crime involving moral turpitude (a 2009/10 false-accounting conviction) plus 212(a)(6)(C)(i) misrepresentation for not disclosing that conviction on a 2018 ESTA application - waiver of inadmissibility explicitly not recommended. The misrepresentation finding (not the underlying old conviction) is what carries the harder-to-overcome, near-lifetime bar; a B-visa waiver requires proven extreme hardship to a US citizen/resident relative, which a business/tourist traveler essentially never has.

Unclear formal grounds - an earlier B1/B2 visa was revoked in 2015 after the applicant sent an angry/threatening Facebook message to a US-based acquaintance who reported her; consulate told her she is not formally 'inadmissible' or permanently banned, yet 9 years later she was refused again on reapplying via ESTA and then a fresh B visa. Shows a revoked visa tied to a reported personal dispute can create a lasting, opaque negative flag that keeps causing denials even without formal inadmissibility.

214(b), 3rd-4th consecutive year - denied despite an active pending K-1 fiance visa petition and documentation (owns property in Costa Rica, expedited request tied to the fiancee's imminent childbirth); officer gave a generic refusal without reviewing submitted paperwork. A sibling's prior deportation for working illegally on a B1/B2 visa likely cast a negative 'family pattern' shadow. A pending K-1 petition does essentially nothing to help a B2 case - if anything it signals immigrant intent.

Initially given a 221(g)/DS-5535 referral (extensive supplemental security questionnaire covering 15 years of travel, addresses and social media) despite strong ties (senior job, extended family, extensive travel history), while his wife with weaker ties (unemployed) was approved instantly the same day. Family suspected his common Muslim name may have triggered a security namecheck. Visa was eventually issued about 8-9 months later, only after the applicant proactively emailed the embassy for a status update.

214(b) - denied despite 10-15 years of stable employment each and a home (though on family land with no property deed in their name) and no debt; the officer specifically asked how many children they have, and denied them immediately after they answered 'one' (their US-based son, the petitioner). Suggests having an only child abroad in the US is treated as a strong pull factor that can override other financial/property ties.

Approved at interview, but the CEAC status tracker briefly showed 'Refused' immediately afterward - a common, poorly-explained placeholder/pending status that later flipped to 'Approved' and then 'Issued' within about a week. Caused significant needless panic; 'Refused' right after an interview does not necessarily mean denied.

214(b) - as soon as the officer learned the applicant's spouse is a US citizen, the interview effectively ended. Strong evidence (permanent employment for both spouses, a specific documented reason for a temporary visit, and a clean prior Schengen travel history) wasn't enough to overcome the presumption once the USC-spouse fact was on the table - reinforcing that a US citizen spouse is treated as such a strong pull factor it can override nearly any tie evidence for a B2.
